[tool_result: 1	# Retelling 01 — Vesta Cobb, a mill hand's daughter, recorded on tape 1974
2	
3	*Tape made for the county's oral-history collection at her kitchen table in Cadder Falls, 1974. Transcribed as spoken; her own doubling-back left in.*
4	
5	Well, you'll have to stop me when you've got enough, because I run on. My husband used to say I could talk the paint off a porch.
6	
7	I was born in nineteen twenty, second house up from the mill gate, and my father was in the mill his whole working life, and my mother's people had been at the Falls since the line was built. Since they were building it, my grandmother would say, because she boarded the men who came in to do it. So I am not from anywhere else, and everything I am going to tell you I got at that stove from people who are all of them dead now.
8	
9	You want to know about the sound. Everybody wants to know about the sound. It has been quiet a long time and now everybody wants it.
10	
11	It was one noise. That is the first thing, and people who never lived here get it wrong — they think it was a rattling or a rolling, like thunder walking off down the valley, and it was not. It was one. One deep report, and then nothing, and the nothing after it was worse than the noise was. Like a door shut in a cellar three towns off. That is how my mother put it and I have never heard it put better. Not sharp like a shot. Deep, the way a big thing sounds when it is a long way down.
12	
13	And you felt it before you heard it. That is the part people don't believe. It came up through the floorboards into your feet, the way the mill did when they started the big saw, only the mill was daytime and this was not. This was always the small hours. Between midnight and four, and I would say closer to two than either end, though I would not swear to it. Nobody heard it at supper. Nobody heard it at noon in their life.
14	
15	And it only came on the killing nights. That was what the Falls called them. Not just cold — we get cold, cold is nothing. It had to be the kind where the day had been soft, shirtsleeve weather almost, mud in the road, and then the sky went hard and clear along about dark and the whole night came to pieces on you. That was a killing night. You could feel it coming at the mill gate at four in the afternoon and my father would come in and say, well, she may talk tonight, and my mother would tell him not to say so in front of the children, and he would say it anyway.
16	
17	Now I heard it. I want that understood, because people my age say they heard it and half of them are repeating their fathers. I heard it.
18	
19	It was a winter in the thirties, and I could not give you the night. We had had rain that day, I remember the rain, and the wash was on the line and it froze on the line, and my mother was cross about it. And that night the whole street came awake at once. Not one house. The whole street. The floor went first, like I said, and then the sound came, and my brother was up before I was and my father was already at the window with no lamp lit. I remember the cold on the glass and I remember there being no wind at all, and dogs going off up and down the row, one after another, and then the dogs quit and it was as still as the inside of a cup. And then doors started opening. Grown men out on their porches in their union suits in that cold, holding their arms, looking up the valley toward the bridge, and not a one of them saying anything, and that is the thing I have never got over. They knew what they were listening for. It was not a surprise to them. It was a visit.
20	
21	My mother put us back to bed and she said, that is only the train, go to sleep, which was the exact wrong thing to say to a child if you wanted her asleep.
22	
23	Because that is what it was. That is what everybody at the Falls knew and I have never had any reason handed to me to think different. Number Nine went into that gorge in the bad winter when the bridge was new, and her crew went in with her, and they we]

[tool_result: 1	# Retelling 02 — Harlan Pike, son of the CVR's chief clerk, from a memoir written in 1958
2	
3	*From "The Company at Ninestone," an unpublished memoir written in his seventies. This chapter, headed "The Sallow Creek Viaduct," is given entire.*
4	
5	My father was chief clerk of the Cadder Valley Railroad from 1893 to 1919, and he brought the office home with him every night of those twenty-six years. Other boys grew up with a dog. I grew up with a stock book. Our dining table on a Sunday was a place where a man might be asked, quite seriously, whether he thought a figure in a column was one the directors would swallow, and I learned to have an opinion before I learned to shave.
6	
7	I set this down because there is nobody left who cares to have it right, and because what is said about the Sallow Creek Viaduct at present is mostly rubbish.
8	
9	Begin with the road, because people who write about the valley never trouble to. The Cadder Valley Railroad was thirty-one miles of it, and no more. Ninestone was milepost 0 — the county seat, the shops, the office, my father's desk with the window on the yard. The Sallow Creek Viaduct stood at milepost 22. Cadder Falls, the mill town, was milepost 23. The Ashby quarry, which was the reason the whole thing existed, was at milepost 31. Everything else the company owned was sidings.
10	
11	The grade from the quarry down to the viaduct was two and two-tenths percent, and it held at that the whole way. I write that plainly because it is the fact from which most of the trouble in this chapter descends. Two and two-tenths percent held all that distance is a great deal of falling for a small railroad with second-hand brakes, and every man on the property knew it, and the company's answer was to hire careful men and pray for cold weather on the drums.
12	
13	The viaduct itself was begun in April 1896 and the line was opened to Cadder Falls on 14 November 1897. It was three spans: one hundred and twenty feet, then a pin-connected truss of three hundred feet across the gorge proper, then one hundred and twenty feet again. Five hundred and forty feet in all, and ninety-seven feet above the water. I have stood on the deck of it as a boy with my father's hand in my collar and I can tell you that ninety-seven feet is a great plenty.
14	
15	Now, the point of the thing, which nobody outside the office ever grasped. Steel moves. It lengthens in the heat and shortens in the cold, and a three-hundred-foot span in a valley that runs from the middle of July to the middle of January moves a good deal. So the center span was pinned solid at its north end and its south end was left free to travel — it rested on a nest of rollers set in a cast pedestal, the south shoe, and the whole span breathed on that nest, out in summer and back in winter, for fifty-odd years.
16	
17	The rule the engineers worked to was one inch in three hundred feet for fifty degrees. That is a rule of thumb and they used it as one; you will find it in any office of that period. For our span, being three hundred feet exactly, it came out at an inch for every fifty degrees, which is the sort of arithmetic even a clerk's son can carry in his head.
18	
19	The span was closed on 12 September 1897 with the thermometer at sixty-six degrees. Sheet 11 of the contract drawings called for four inches of travel on the south nest. Four inches was generous for a three-hundred-foot span, and I have always thought it showed a proper caution in whoever drew it.
20	
21	The resident engineer on the work was Warren Tice, afterward the company's chief engineer at Ninestone and a considerable man in this county. The party's computer was a Miss Adela Rennick. She did the arithmetic, and she did it better than the party did — that is my father's phrase, not mine, and he was not a man who handed out compliments to save postage. She kept her own duplicate book, in her own hand, quite separate from the party's book, which was thought eccentric and was not. Her time]

r02 — Harlan Pike's 1958 memoir chapter: company records rebutting r01 — the March 6, 1898 wreck killed no one and Engine No. 9 was later sold running in 1901; he blames the "sound" on the 1908 re-decking overloading the bridge's roller bearings, ending when they were replaced in 1954.

[tool_result: 1	# Retelling 03 — Judd Rennick, station agent (retired), interviewed at his kitchen table, 1965
2	
3	*Recorded for the Pell County Historical Society. The interviewer's questions have been dropped; his answers are printed as he gave them.*
4	
5	I was born in eighty-eight, here. My father was Emil Rennick. He was a carpenter and he built the falsework for that bridge, which is the timber they stand the iron on until the iron will stand by itself. Then you knock the timber down. He was proud of it and he never got a line of credit for it anywhere.
6	
7	My father had a younger sister, Adela. She worked for the same railroad before I was born, in the engineering party, out in the field with the men. She never spoke about it. Not to me, not once. I asked her twice when I was a boy and got nothing, and after that I had better sense.
8	
9	I went on nights in 1907 and I started the book that same winter. Then they made me agent. Thirty-nine years at that depot, all told. I have been out of it a good while now and I still wake at four.
10	
11	You want to know about the sound. I will tell you what it was like and then I will tell you what I do not know, and I would be obliged if you would print both.
12	
13	It was one report. Deep. It was not a rattle and it was not a roll and it did not travel — it was there and then it was done. And it came up the rails first. That is the part I have never got anybody to believe who was not sitting where I sat. The sounder on my table would rattle in its bracket before the sound got to the room. A little dry rattle, like a bug in a box. Then the floor. Then the noise. I timed that gap once with a watch and could not get a reading on it, it is that short, but the order never changed in forty-three winters.
14	
15	It was always between midnight and four. Never in the evening. Never at daylight. Between midnight and four.
16	
17	The first time she spoke was the winter of 1913. I was on nights, alone in the office, and I thought a car had got away in the quarry and come down on us. I went out on the platform with a lantern and there was nothing wrong anywhere and it was so cold the lantern glass cracked. In the morning I ruled up a book.
18	
19	Five columns. The date. The day's high. The night's low. Whether she spoke. And the hour. That is all. I did not put down what I thought about it because what I thought about it was not worth the ink, and because a man who writes down his opinion once will write down his opinion instead of the reading the next time. Forty-three winters of that.
20	
21	Now the conditions, and I did not have these at the start. I got them out of the book after a good many winters, when there was enough of it to look at.
22	
23	She never spoke unless the night's low went below six degrees. Never once. Not at seven, not at six and a half. Below six.
24	
25	And she never spoke unless the day before had been at least thirty degrees warmer than the night that followed. It had to fall thirty. A cold night on the end of a cold day was nothing to her. It had to be a soft day and then the bottom out of it.
26	
27	Both, every time. There is not an exception in the book, and I would know, because I went through it looking for one.
28	
29	Here are the totals and I will stand on them. Sixty-one nights she spoke. Thirty-four winters she spoke at least once. Nine winters she never spoke at all — the nine and the thirty-four make the forty-three, you can check me. And five nights answered both conditions and gave nothing. So sixty-six nights answered them in all, and on five of the sixty-six she kept still.
30	
31	I know why the five were silent, or I think I do, and this is the only guess of mine I will let you have. She would not speak twice inside one freeze. Once she had spoken she was done until there had been a thaw — a real thaw, up above forty in the daytime, not a mild hour at noon. Every one of the five silent nights sits in a cold spell where she had already spoken and where nothing had ]

r03 — Judd Rennick's 1965 interview: his 43-winter log with exact data (61 nights spoke, two strict conditions — low below 6°F and a 30°+ overnight drop; 7 of 190 deaths followed within a week), the wager story confirmed, and the sound stopping after 1953 rocker bearings replaced the old pedestals — noting an internal date wrinkle (his slate quote says "August 1909" but he then calls it "the summer of 1911").

[tool_result: 1	# Retelling 04 — Ruth Frayne, "What the Creek Gave Back," a talk to the Pell County Historical Society, 1963
2	
3	*Read to the Society at Ninestone; her blackboard figures are given in the text.*
4	
5	Thank you. I am an engineer with the Pell County highway department, three years in it, and I did not go out to Sallow Creek last September to settle anything. I went because the creek was going to be dry, and a dry creek under a railroad bridge is an opportunity that does not come twice in a career. The state's flood-control cut took Sallow Creek out of its bed for eleven weeks and the gorge was dry to the gravel. The inspection was routine, and stopped being routine on the second afternoon.
6	
7	I have four findings and then some arithmetic, and I would ask you to hold your questions until the arithmetic, which is where the talk is going.
8	
9	**Finding one is nothing.** I walked the bed for something over eight hundred feet, above and below the viaduct, and there is no locomotive in Sallow Creek. There is no frame, no boiler shell, no driving wheel, nothing of iron larger than a spike. The photographs are on the table at the back. I state it flatly because it required no interpretation: I went and looked and it is not there.
10	
11	**Finding two is the pedestal.** Forty feet below the abutment on the south side, lying in the gravel where the 1954 gang threw it over, is a casting the size of a kitchen stove. It is the old south shoe of the center span — the pedestal that carried the roller nest.
12	
13	Why that matters: a three-hundred-foot steel span gets longer when hot and shorter when cold, and has to be allowed to. The center span is pinned at the north end and free at the south, and the south end used to ride on rollers in that casting. Cut into the roller seat is a chisel mark — the setting mark, where the nest was to be placed at erection so that there would be room for the steel to come back in the cold. I measured it three times with a steel tape and got the same answer each time. The chisel mark is at two inches. The bearings that were put in in 1954, which are rockers, not rollers, measure four inches of travel each way, and I measured those too.
14	
15	**Finding three is my grandmother's field book.** Adela Rennick, born 1874, died 1959 at eighty-five, was a computer and rodman for the railroad's engineering party while the viaduct was building. She kept her own duplicate of the party's book, in black oilcloth, all her life. It came to my father, Wendell Frayne, when she died, and he gave it to me when I said I was going out to the creek.
16	
17	In the front matter of that book, among the tables, is one line:
18	
19	> *Rule for the long span: one inch in three hundred feet for forty degrees.*
20	
21	That is the working rule for the movement of that steel. Three hundred feet of it, an inch for every forty degrees. Remember that line; everything else follows from it.
22	
23	And on page sixty-two:
24	
25	> *Sept. 12, 1897. Span closed 3:40 p.m., thermometer 66°. Rollers set at the two-inch mark. Sheet 11 calls for three. Reported to W.T., who answers that the pedestal cannot be recast before the fall haul and that two inches is more than the valley will ever ask for. Entered here so that it is somewhere. — A.R.*
26	
27	She reported it. She was overruled. She wrote it down so that it would be somewhere, and there it sat for sixty-five years while the valley told itself a ghost story.
28	
29	**Finding four is the night book**, which my father's uncle, Judd Rennick, lent me himself. He is seventy-four, he lives three streets from the depot he kept as station agent at Cadder Falls, and he wrote down every occurrence of the sound the valley called the boom, in a ruled book, for forty-three winters. Sixty-one nights. On every one the night's low was below six degrees above zero, and stood at the bottom of a fall of thirty degrees or more from the day's high. Further nights answered both conditions and produced nothing at ]

r04 — Ruth Frayne's 1963 engineering talk: hard evidence — no locomotive in the creek; recovered pedestal shows a 2-inch chisel mark vs. Sheet 11's 3-inch spec; grandmother Adela Rennett's field book (1-inch-per-40°F rule, overruled 1897 report) plus Judd's night-book conditions math to a binding point of -14°F before the 1909 re-decking and +6°F after it, with Kettle Bench weather records confirming onset began January 1912 — not 1897-98 as legend held.

[tool_result: 1	# Retelling 05 — Alma Nace, "The Engines My Grandfather Bought," a memoir for the Bly County annual, 1970
2	
3	*Written at the editor's asking by the founder's granddaughter, sixty-three, who grew up inside the sound of the engines and remembers her mother's ledgers the way other people remember furniture.*
4	
5	The editor wants the engines. I will get to the engines. But you cannot start a Tolliver story with an engine any more than you can start a tree with a board, so you will have to take my grandfather first.
6	
7	Silas Tolliver was born in 1849 and came into this county with a mill, a horse, and a conviction that the horse was temporary. That is the whole man in one sentence and I have never found a better one. The mill he built twice, the second time out of the first one's lumber. The horse he kept for years and complained about for every one of them. He died in 1922 in the chair by the office stove, and my mother said afterward that he had spent his whole life getting the horse out of his business and then went and left it in his obituary anyway, because the paper led with the horse.
8	
9	The Sixmile tram was named for the creek and not for its length, which is a thing I have had to explain to visitors my whole life. It began at about that length, I grant you, but it did not stay there. By the end it was nineteen miles of thirty-pound rail running up three drainages, with switchbacks where the ground would not take a curve, and grades that the men described in language my mother would not enter in a book. The rail was light and the ties were whatever came off the hill nearest, and it hauled more timber than anything in this county before or since.
10	
11	My mother, Pearl Tolliver Nace, was born in 1881 and kept the company's books from the age of eighteen, which is to say for thirty-nine years, because she was better at it than anybody her father could hire. That is not my phrase. That is the phrase he used, in front of company, and she never once let on that she liked hearing it.
12	
13	Now. In 1901 my grandfather decided he wanted a road engine. What he had were geared machines that could climb anything and could not be hurried, and what he wanted was something with big wheels and a long wheelbase that would bring a made-up train of loads down the main stem faster than a man could walk beside it. He was very specific about that. Faster than walking. He had watched his own timber walk for twenty years and he was done with it.
14	
15	It was my mother who found her. There was an advertisement from a railroad down in Pell County, a little branch line selling off a twelve-year-old American-type engine, and Pearl put it on the desk without a word and went back to her column. She was a 4-4-0 out of the Rowan Works, built in 1889, works number 1142. She had cost her first owners eight thousand six hundred dollars new — my mother wrote that figure in the margin of the page, and my grandfather repeated the comparison for the rest of his life to anybody who would hold still. We paid two thousand five hundred and ten dollars for her. That was in 1902.
16	
17	Delivered on her own wheels, was the phrase, and my grandfather said it so often that I did not understand as a child what a fine thing it was. It meant she came north under her own steam — eleven days and four railroads, with a Pell County crew who handed her over at the interchange, drank coffee in our kitchen, and turned around and went home on the cars like passengers. My mother fed them. She said the fireman was the politest man she ever met and had a burn on his wrist he would not talk about.
18	
19	The shop painted out the 9 and painted on a 4, because the company numbered its engines in the order it bought them and never once in the order of their merit. So she was No. 4 from that season onward, and everybody called her the Four, and nobody under thirty knew she had ever been anything else.
20	
21	She was a disappointment for exactly one season. They put her on gra]

[tool_result: 1	# Retelling 06 — Lettie Wexler, "A Farm Book of Weather," a reminiscence for a farm journal, 1965
2	
3	*Written at seventy-six by the keeper of the Kettle Bench weather record, at the journal's request, for a series on farm records kept in one family.*
4	
5	There is not much to tell and I will not stretch it.
6	
7	Our place is Kettle Bench, three miles up the valley from Cadder Falls, on the shoulder above the creek where the frost sits longer than it does in town. My father was Peter Wexler. He began the weather record in 1884 and kept it until 1926, and I have kept it since, which makes eighty-one years of it, now, in one hand or the other.
8	
9	It is three figures a day and nothing else. The day's high. The night's low. The rain, or the snow measured melted. My father set the thermometer on the north wall of the milk house where the sun never touches it and it has never been moved. The reading is taken at daylight and again at four, and the low is the low at daylight unless the night was strange, in which case you say so in the margin and do not argue about it.
10	
11	I have not missed a morning since 1926. I have taken it with a broken wrist and I have taken it the morning after my father's funeral, and people think that is remarkable and it is not. It is only that a record with a hole in it is not a record. It is a story about the weather, and there are enough of those.
12	
13	Which brings me to the thing your readers will want, so I may as well come to it.
14	
15	We were related to nobody in this business — not to the railroad people, not to the mill people, not to the Cadder Falls families that the tale belongs to. My father had no interest in the bridge and neither have I. In eighty-odd years of pages there is not one word about it, because we never wrote down a noise. We wrote down weather. That turns out to have been worth something, though it was not why we did it.
16	
17	In 1962 the Frayne girl came up the hill. Ruth Frayne, the engineer — she does the county's road surveys, and she was working down at the creek that fall. She wanted the whole record. I gave it to her in four cardboard boxes, which is what it comes to, and she brought every box back, which I will say for her, because not everybody does.
18	
19	She asked me first for one date, the seventeenth of January, 1912, and I found it for her while she stood there. It is in my father's hand:
20	
21	> *Jan. 17. High 34. Low −2 at daylight. Clear, still.*
22	
23	Thirty-six degrees of fall in a day, and clear and still after it. That is the kind of night the cold comes down out of the sky and just sits.
24	
25	Then she asked for something harder, which was the twelve years after the line opened — from the winter of 1897 and 1898 through to the summer of 1909. I went through it page by page over two evenings. In those twelve years there were seven nights below six degrees. Four of the seven came after days at least thirty degrees warmer than the night that followed. The coldest reading of the whole twelve years was nine below, on the fourth of February, 1899. I remember writing that out for her twice because she wanted the date as well as the figure.
26	
27	She asked about the two winters after that, too, and those are easy, because there is nothing in them. The winter of 1909 and 1910 and the winter of 1910 and 1911 never went below nine above zero, either one of them, and the coldest morning of the pair was the third of February, 1911. That is a mild pair of winters for this valley and I have no explanation for them except that we got them.
28	
29	The hard one was 1917 and 1918. That is the deepest cold anybody up here ever wrote down. Eleven below zero, in January of 1918, and that is the lowest figure in the whole series from my father's first page to this morning's. The high side of it belongs to July of 1936: one hundred and one degrees, which I took myself and did not believe, and took again an hour later.
30	
31	Now, the station agent down at Cadder Fal]

r06 — Lettie Wexler's 1965 farm-journal piece: her family's independent Kettle Bench weather record (1884-present) cross-validates Judd's conditions night-for-night, but her recollection of his book's "silent" nights (8, for 69 total) conflicts with Judd's own count in r03 (5 silent, 66 total) — and her "lowest ever" reading of -11°F (Jan 1918) conflicts with r04's -13°F for the same month/record.

[tool_result: 1	# Retelling 07 — Merrit Sable, curator, accession notes, Pell County Historical Society, Ninestone, 1970
2

## Section A — Reconstruction

### A1. The building of the Sallow Creek Viaduct

The Cadder Valley Railroad (CVR) ran 31 miles from Ninestone (milepost 0, the county seat) to the Ashby quarry (milepost 31). Its principal structure, the Sallow Creek Viaduct at milepost 22, was begun in April 1896: three spans — 120 feet, a 300-foot pin-connected center truss, and 120 feet — totaling 540 feet, 97 feet above the creek. The line opened to Cadder Falls (milepost 23) on 14 November 1897. The resident engineer was Warren Tice, later the CVR's chief engineer at Ninestone; Emil Rennick built the timber falsework; the party's "computer" (rodman and calculator) was Emil's younger sister, Adela Rennick.

Steel expands and contracts with temperature, so the center span was pinned solid at its north end and left free at the south, riding on a nest of rollers in a cast pedestal. The governing rule, recorded in Adela's own field book, was one inch of travel per 300 feet for every 40°F of change. Sheet 11 of the contract drawings called for 3 inches of travel in the south nest. The span was closed on 12 September 1897 at 3:40 p.m. with the steel at 66°F — but the rollers were set to only a 2-inch mark, because, per Adela's book, the pedestal could not be recast before the fall haul. She reported the shortfall to Tice ("W.T."), was overruled, and wrote it down anyway "so that it is somewhere." A family story passed down at two removes (Emil to Adela to her son) has Tice privately admitting at his 1931 retirement dinner, "we set that nest a mark shy and I have listened to it ever since"; his son Dorsey Tice denies this was ever said.
